_comment: The guided tour (tour.js in the app, tour.html as slides and PDF). One file drives all three, so the words are written once. In the app the tour is a walk through the site: each view a step opens is a stop, where a card names the step, gives its headline and says what to try (hint). A headline is one figure (value, label) or a comparison (figures, each with its label), and may lead with a claim it supports and say what was measured (measure); a step that opens no view is one card on its own. Numbers are never typed here where the data can say them: a {placeholder} is filled at runtime from data/boundary_evidence.json and the published journey-times index (tourFigureValues in tour-figures.js), so a weekly rebuild cannot leave the tour quoting stale figures. A typed figure names its source and the date it was checked. preview_only would keep the tour behind ?preview=1; it is public from 3 November 2026. Rewritten on 3 November 2026 at the maintainer's request to show what the platform does, step by step, with the boundary evidence as one step of ten. The menu's badge shows until event.show_until.

opening.headline: Every bus on this coast: live, measured and open.
opening.lead: Four bus companies, the trains and the coaches, on one map, one departure board and one ticket checker, built entirely from the government's open bus data. It also keeps what the buses actually did, so anyone can see how each route really runs.

steps.title: Every bus on one map
steps.lead: Every operator's buses, live, with the trains and coaches that share the coast.

headline.label: Brighton & Hove, Metrobus, Stagecoach and Compass, on one live map

points: Bus positions from the Bus Open Data Service, refreshed every 20 seconds, for every operator in the area.
Each bus drawn in its own livery, from the vehicle list kept by bustimes.org.
Trains from Realtime Trains, FlixBus and National Express coaches, and rail replacement buses, on the same map.
Tap a bus for the stops still ahead of it, when it is expected at each, the journey it runs next, and its route's registration history.

try.label: Every bus, live
try.hint: Each bus is drawn in its own livery. Tap one for the stops it has still to call at and when it is expected.

sources.label: Bus Open Data Service: "free open data, and does not require a licence"
bustimes.org: the vehicle list behind each bus's livery

steps.title: One departure board for every operator
steps.lead: Any stop's departures from every operator, in time order, with live, estimated and timetabled times marked apart.

headline.label: with one board for every operator calling there

points: Live times from the operator's own prediction where there is one, else our estimate from where the bus is, else the timetable, and always labelled.
Our estimates lean early: a late bus is assumed to stay most of that late, so you are more likely to wait than to miss it.
A live time before a bus sets off, from the journey that bus is finishing now.
Diversions and closed stops from the operators' own notices, with the nearest stop still served.
When buses run here each day, the last bus home, and the stop's shelter, seating and step-free access.

try.label: One board, every operator
try.name: St Peter's Church
try.hint: Brighton & Hove, Metrobus, Stagecoach and Compass in one list. Tap any departure to see where that bus is now.

try.label: Plan a journey (experimental)
try.hint: Door to door, across operators. Experimental, so check before you travel.

steps.title: Every route, day and night
steps.lead: The whole network drawn from the published timetables, or any one route with its stops, notices, tickets and its own performance report.

headline.label: drawn from the timetables, by day or by night

points: Every route on one map, coloured by operator, with a Night buses view of what runs after dark.
Choose an operator and a route for its stops each way, when it runs today, the notices in force and the tickets valid on it.
Each route we track links to its route report: punctuality, waiting and where time is lost, week by week.
Tap any stop for every service calling there and how often.

try.label: The whole network
try.hint: Every route, coloured by operator. Switch to Night buses to see what runs after dark.

try.label: One route: the 700
try.hint: The 700's stops each way, when it runs today, its notices and tickets. Open its route report for punctuality and where it loses time.

steps.title: The cheapest ticket, whatever the operator
steps.lead: Each operator's ticket zones on one map, and a checker that finds the cheapest way to cover a whole journey, across companies.

headline.label: the cheapest ticket that covers the whole journey

points: Every operator's day-ticket zones drawn on the map.
The cheapest combination for a journey, including tickets valid on more than one operator, weekly tickets and capped single fares.
Single fares by route, from the operators' published fare tables.
Where a change in ticketing would make a journey cheaper, the checker says by how much.

try.hint: The cheapest ticket that covers the whole journey, across companies. Change either stop to try your own.

steps.title: What the buses actually did
steps.lead: The live feed, kept every minute and matched to the timetable: real journey times, where buses lose time, and a printable report for every route we track.

headline.label: of the live feed kept and matched to the timetable

points: Each minute the live feed is saved, and each bus is matched to the timetabled journey it is running.
Journey times between any two stops, by day and time of day, with the slow end shown as well as the usual.
Waiting, bunching and punctuality at the boarding stop, once enough complete days are recorded.
A delay map of where buses lose time; a stretch is coloured only once it has enough journeys behind it.
Gaps in the record are listed, not hidden: {recorded_gaps}.

try.label: Worthing to Portslade, measured
try.hint: Each dot is one bus we timed from Worthing to Portslade, across the council line. The solid line is the usual time and the dashed line the timetable. Change the day or the time of day to compare.

try.label: Where buses lose time
try.hint: Each stretch is coloured by the time buses lose there. Tap one for its figures.

steps.title: How far to trust it
steps.lead: Every figure says what it was divided by, how it was made, and what would make it wrong.

headline.claim: The live times on this site are closer to when the bus really leaves than the timetable is.
headline.measure: How often each was within the accuracy window the Real Time Information Group (RTIG) recommends, replayed over 28 recorded days (25 September to 24 October), outside recorded disruptions.

points: As the board actually showed them, minute by minute, on ordinary days 79% of live times were within RTIG's window, and 86% of departures had a live time 15 minutes before they were due. We publish how often we are wrong, nightly, on the live data health page.
Fewer than 10 journeys over 5 days shows "too few", never a number.
{identified_share}% of {identified_tracked} tracked journeys are matched to their journey by the operator's own feed.
Stop times are being checked by hand at the roadside; the result will be published here.
A bus we did not see is "missing", never "cancelled": its tracker may simply have been off.

sources.label: Live estimates judged by RTIG's windows: 28 recorded days replayed (25 October 2026)

Passenger reports and notes, and a form to tell us about something we have missed.

steps.title: Where the network falls short
steps.lead: The same data shows where the network serves people less well. On this coast, services west of the council boundary at Portslade are weaker on every measure.

headline.claim: The council border between West Sussex and Brighton & Hove has a measurable impact on passenger services west of the line.
headline.measure: Average weekday buses per stop, over every stop within 4 km of the line along the coast. The west gets {band_share}% of the east's service.

figures.label: West of the line, in West Sussex
East of the line, in Brighton & Hove

points: Weekday departures per stop: {band_west_dps} west of the line against {band_east_dps} east, in a band 4 km either side ({band_share}%).
Routes on a weekday: {routes_west_weekday} against {routes_east_weekday}. On Saturday {routes_west_sat} against {routes_east_sat}; on Sunday {routes_west_sun} against {routes_east_sun}.
Departures after 11pm on a weekday: {late_west} west of the line against {late_east} east.
Lancing and South Portslade, about five miles apart on the same coast road: {lancing_dps} against {sportslade_dps} weekday departures per stop.
Joint working pays: up to 43% more passengers on the two routes the councils improved together. The coast west of Portslade wasn't one of them.
Better buses sets out what would help, who is responsible for each change and how far it has got, and drafts a letter to your councillor.

steps.title: Open, accessible and cheap to run
steps.lead: No login and no app to install. Built for every reader, from open data, under an open licence.

headline.label: a year to run: the data is free, and so is the hosting

points: Accessible by design: dark mode, larger text, reduced motion and colour-blind-safe colours, with every control reachable by keyboard.
ABOD, the Department's free analytics service, is for operators and councils, by invitation. This is open to everyone, and joins the evidence to passenger tools.
ABOD matches a bus to its journey one way and skips it when that fails. This site tries three ways, and names {identified_share}% of tracked journeys by the operator's own feed.
ABOD's code may be reused only by KPMG firms. This site's code is MIT-licensed, its words and data are CC BY, and every day's evidence is archived in public.
The data is free and so is the hosting: under £20 a year, the cost of the web address. A template for other regions is on the way.

sources.label: Bus Open Data Service: "free open data, and does not require a licence"
Render: the free instance type the live data runs on

steps.lead: The code is open and the data is public. Operators: check our figures. Councils: plan the coast as one corridor. Other regions and technology firms: help turn this into a template.
